title: EATSON v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary: In Eatson v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Eatson, a British national born into a Gypsy family and living a traditional nomadic lifestyle, brought a case against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities—specifically, the harm caused by planning laws that restrict their ability to live according to their cultural traditions. For over a decade, Ms. Eatson and her family faced repeated evictions and harassment by authorities as they travelled in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire. After purchasing land in Tilsworth to establish a nursery business, they were denied permanent planning permission to live in a caravan on their own land, despite their clear Gypsy identity and lack of suitable alternative accommodation. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), acknowledging that the planning decisions interfered with Ms. Eatson’s ability to maintain her identity and way of life. However, the Court found the application inadmissible, holding that the interference pursued a legitimate aim—environmental protection—and that national authorities had a wide margin of appreciation in balancing these interests. This case is significant as it reflects the ongoing tension between environmental policies and the rights of Roma and Traveller communities, at a time when European states were only beginning to grapple with the need for culturally sensitive planning laws.
